solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Challenged wicked madcap (9)

blocks.note: to dare someone is to challenge them
evil = wicked

annotation.surface: Someone has thrown down a challenge to a reckless wild person.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end: 'madcap' is a noun here, a reckless person, not the adjective the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: A daredevil is a reckless person who takes wild risks, which is what a madcap is.

entries.clue: Took glasses, finally spotted where taxi might be (5)

indicatorNotes.finally: takes the final letter of the next word

blocks.note: last letter of spotted
a taxi rank is where cabs wait for fares

annotation.surface: Someone put on their spectacles and at last saw a spot for a cab.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Took glasses' looks like putting on spectacles; it means drank, glasses of drink. A taxi rank is the British name for a cab stand.
annotation.definitionFit: To take glasses, as in glasses of wine, is to drink them.

entries.clue: Lodge retains for all to see what’s not been taken (7)

indicatorNotes.retains: the first word holds the next piece inside it

blocks.note: to lodge somewhere is to reside there
U is the film certificate for universal viewing, suitable for everyone

annotation.surface: A club lodge keeps on public display whatever nobody claimed.
annotation.walkthrough: U is the British film classification meaning universal: suitable for all to see. 'Lodge' is a verb here, not a club building.
annotation.definitionFit: Residue is a plain synonym for the leftovers, whatever remains once the rest has been taken away.

entries.clue: Prod grandad struggling to move on-screen (4,3,4)

indicatorNotes.struggling: the letters labour into a new arrangement

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: Nudge an elderly relative who is having trouble using a computer mouse.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a very recognisable scene: grandad wrestling with a computer, which is exactly where the answer belongs.
annotation.definitionFit: To drag and drop is to move an item on a computer screen by holding and releasing it with the mouse.

entries.clue: Tourist destination is jolly pleasant without Rodney on vacation (6)

indicatorNotes.without: the following letters are taken out
indicatorNotes.on vacation: Rodney is emptied of its middle, leaving only its outer letters

blocks.note: jolly = very, pleasant = nice
RODNEY with its insides vacated leaves R…Y, which comes out of VERY

annotation.surface: A holiday spot would be lovely if only Rodney were not coming along.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' is British for very, as in jolly good. Remove RY from VE(RY) NICE.
annotation.definitionFit: Venice is one of the world's most visited tourist cities.

entries.clue: Sweet to sprawl with one soft drink (8)

blocks.note: to loll is to sprawl lazily
I = one, the Roman numeral
pop = fizzy soft drink

annotation.surface: A treat is to lounge about with a fizzy drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' is the British word for a piece of candy, here a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: 'sweet' is British for a piece of candy, and this is one on a stick.

entries.clue: Sober report’s conclusion mentioned arrests (5)

indicatorNotes.conclusion: takes the end letter of report
indicatorNotes.arrests: the outer word catches and holds the letter inside it

blocks.note: said = mentioned
last letter of report

annotation.surface: A serious-minded summary of police arrests at the end of a report.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Arrests' reads as police business but is only the containment instruction, and 'mentioned' is a synonym here, not a sound-alike signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Staid means sober and sedate in manner.

entries.clue: In this state because divorced from church? (3)

indicatorNotes.divorced from: separated from, so the church letters are removed

blocks.note: since = because
CE = Church of England, removed from SINCE

annotation.surface: A couple are in a particular condition because they split from the church.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is 'living in sin': a couple together without a church wedding. CE is the standard abbreviation for Church of England.
annotation.definitionFit: Living in sin is the state of cohabiting unmarried, as the question mark signals.

entries.clue: From thieves he stole a large cake — I tucked in (3,4)

indicatorNotes.tucked in: I is tucked into the middle of the other pieces

blocks.note: a as written
L = large, the clothing size
a baba is a rum-soaked yeast cake
I as written, tucked in between L and BABA

annotation.surface: A cake thief confesses to eating a large one himself.
annotation.walkthrough: In the Arabian Nights tale, Ali Baba robs the treasure cave of the forty thieves; the definition has no helpful synonym to lean on.
annotation.definitionFit: Ali Baba stole treasure from the forty thieves' cave.

entries.clue: One may be given a lead to follow arrest (3,6)

annotation.definition: One may be given a lead

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely
to collar a suspect is to arrest them

annotation.surface: A detective receives a tip-off to shadow a suspect and make an arrest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like a clue from police work, but it is a dog's leash, clipped to the collar. Both wordplay words are police slang.
annotation.definitionFit: A dog collar is the thing a leash is attached to.

entries.clue: Duck out? A black mark (7)

blocks.note: a as written
B = black, as on pencils
a stain is a mark

annotation.surface: A cricketer out for a duck is a black mark on the scorecard.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket, a duck is a score of nought; the surface plays on that, but 'Duck out' is simply to avoid taking part.
annotation.definitionFit: To abstain is to duck out of voting or taking part.

entries.clue: Inspiring object keeps spirit attacking in combat (7)

indicatorNotes.keeps: the first piece holds the second inside

blocks.note: a lung is the organ that inspires, breathes in
gin is a spirit, sitting inside the organ's name just before its last letter

annotation.surface: A motivating keepsake keeps a fighter's courage up in battle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Inspiring' is literal: to inspire is to breathe in, which is what a lung does.
annotation.definitionFit: Lunging is thrusting forward to strike, as in fencing or a fight.

entries.clue: Family giving away new child (3)

indicatorNotes.giving away: gives up a letter, so N is removed

blocks.note: kind = family, sort, as in 'of that kind'
N = new, removed from KIND

annotation.surface: A family puts a newborn up for adoption.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an adoption story; the letter-level instruction is just KIND losing its N.
annotation.definitionFit: Kid is the everyday informal synonym for a child, borrowed from the word for a young goat.

entries.clue: Chop Algeria into bits making group of islands (11)

indicatorNotes.into bits: the letters are broken up and reassembled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: Break a country up into pieces to make a string of islands.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chop' reads as the anagram instruction, but it is fodder; the indicator is 'into bits'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word began as the Greek name for the island-strewn Aegean Sea.

entries.clue: Deviously vet earnings for western luminary (7,4)

indicatorNotes.Deviously: by a crooked route, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: Someone crookedly checks the income of a Hollywood western film star.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Western luminary' sounds like a cowboy film star; it is Venus, seen low in the western sky after sunset.
annotation.definitionFit: The evening star is Venus shining in the west at dusk.

entries.clue: What widow used to wear on back of smart clothes (6)

indicatorNotes.back of: the rear, so the last letter

blocks.note: last letter of smart
widow's weeds were the black mourning clothes

annotation.surface: A widow's traditional dress, worn on the back of fashionable clothing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Widow's weeds' is the old phrase for mourning dress. Here 'on' means placed after: T then WEEDS.
annotation.definitionFit: Tweeds are clothes made of tweed cloth, typical country wear.

entries.clue: Celebrating success of president hosting current prince (9)

indicatorNotes.hosting: the president holds the next letter inside

blocks.note: Donald Trump, US president
I is the symbol for electric current, inside TRUMP: TR(I)UMP
Prince Hal, Shakespeare's young Henry V

annotation.surface: A president throws a party for a young royal to mark a victory.
annotation.walkthrough: I for current is from physics; Hal is the stock crossword prince from Shakespeare's Henry IV plays.
annotation.definitionFit: Triumphal means celebrating a victory or success, as in a triumphal arch.

entries.clue: Joint parliament welcomes old retired soldier (8)

indicatorNotes.welcomes: the parliament takes the others in

blocks.note: the Dáil is the lower house of the Irish parliament
O = old
a vet is a veteran, a soldier who has left the service

annotation.surface: A combined assembly greets an elderly former serviceman.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Joint' tempts as an adjective (joint parliament); it is a woodworking noun. 'Retired' is not a reversal: VET stays as written.
annotation.definitionFit: A dovetail is an interlocking woodwork joint shaped like a dove's tail.

entries.clue: Chap was out front nursing a cold, severely restricted (8)

indicatorNotes.nursing: the outer pieces hold the next letters, as a nurse holds a patient

blocks.note: a chap is a man
a as written
C = cold, as on taps
to lead is to be out in front

annotation.surface: A man was leading the race despite battling a cold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nursing a cold' paints an invalid, but it is a container: the chap and 'was out front' together hold the two letters between them.
annotation.definitionFit: Manacles are handcuffs or shackles, so someone in them has their movement severely restricted.

entries.clue: Licentious closing time never forgotten (8)

indicatorNotes.closing: enclosing, shutting the next letter inside

blocks.note: licentious = immoral
T = time, the physics symbol, shut inside the first word

annotation.surface: At a rowdy late-night pub, last orders is a moment nobody forgets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Closing time' looks like one unit, a pub's last orders; split it, and 'closing' means enclosing. Not the last letter of time.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in its figurative sense: great artists are called this because their fame never dies.

entries.clue: Two family members in charge of craft (7)

blocks.note: MA (mother) and SON
IC = in charge

annotation.surface: Two relatives run a boat, or a family business.
annotation.walkthrough: Freemasons call their brotherhood 'the Craft', so masonic means 'of the Craft'; 'craft' misleads toward boats or handiwork.
annotation.definitionFit: Masonic means relating to Freemasonry, known to its members as the Craft.

entries.clue: One scorching vocalist (6)

blocks.note: someone who singes things, read literally
a vocalist is a performer who uses their voice

annotation.surface: A red-hot performer on stage.
annotation.walkthrough: Two senses, one spelling: the vocalist, and a person who singes, though that one is said differently.
annotation.definitionFit: One sense is the everyday word for a vocalist; the other is the literal 'one who singes', from the verb to singe.

entries.clue: Managed in holiday cottage? It’s very hard (7)

annotation.definitionNote: a description of the answer rather than a synonym: granite is what is very hard

indicatorNotes.in: the first piece goes inside the second

blocks.note: a gîte is a French holiday cottage
ran = managed, as in ran a business; it goes inside the cottage

annotation.surface: Running a holiday let is a tough business.
annotation.walkthrough: GÎTE, a rented French country cottage, is a crossword regular.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this rock is the stock example of something very hard, as in 'granite-faced'.

entries.clue: Wife is top American beauty? (6)

blocks.note: informal British word for a wife
the title of the winner of the national US beauty pageant, split into two words

annotation.surface: A husband boasts that his wife is the best-looking woman in America.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer as MISS US, the title of America's top beauty queen; the question mark flags the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal British slang for a wife; split in two, it also reads as Miss US, America's top beauty queen.

entries.clue: Teacher at her best using bad language (11)

blocks.note: pupils call a female teacher Miss
peaking = at one's best

annotation.surface: A teacher is on top form while swearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bad language' suggests swearing; here it means speaking wrongly.
annotation.definitionFit: Misspeaking is using the wrong words, speaking badly.

entries.clue: One punches everyone in the ear (3)

indicatorNotes.in the ear: as heard, so a word that sounds the same

blocks.note: all = everyone; its sound matches a tool spelt differently

annotation.surface: Someone hits everybody on the side of the head.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Punches' suggests a boxer; an awl punches holes in leather.
annotation.definitionFit: An awl is a pointed tool for punching holes.

entries.clue: Insult snubbing leader is not serious (5)

blocks.note: a slight is an insult; drop its leading S

annotation.surface: A slight that ignores the boss is not meant seriously.
annotation.walkthrough: SLIGHT loses its S. 'Snubbing' fits the insult picture while doing the cutting.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of light reading or entertainment, meant to amuse rather than weigh on you.

entries.clue: Pass on nasty flu, one hard to control (7)

indicatorNotes.nasty: the letters are in a bad way, so rearranged

blocks.note: to hand something on is to pass it
anagram of flu

annotation.surface: A troublesome child is passing on a bad cold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' just places HAND before the rearranged FLU.
annotation.definitionFit: A handful is a person who is difficult to manage.

entries.clue: Whimsical female you once upset (3)

indicatorNotes.upset: in a down clue, turned upside down, so reversed

blocks.note: F = female
ye is the old word for you

annotation.surface: A quirky woman once upset you.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks an archaic word: YE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word describes someone quirky and otherworldly, a little away with the fairies.

entries.clue: This writer’s work is getting harder (7)

blocks.note: 'this writer' is the crossword compiler, whose job is making puzzles
what concrete or jelly does as it hardens

annotation.surface: The crossword compiler admits the puzzles are becoming tougher.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter of the puzzle in front of you, so his work is setting. 'Harder' is physical, not more difficult.
annotation.definitionFit: Setting is what a crossword setter does, and also what cement does as it hardens.

entries.clue: Brave, but not to start with, like Jim in novel? (5)

indicatorNotes.not to start with: 'not to start with' says the word goes without its opening, so the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: plucky = brave; drop the P

annotation.surface: A cowardly hero turns brave, like a character in a book.
annotation.walkthrough: Lucky Jim is Kingsley Amis's 1954 comic novel about a hapless young lecturer.
annotation.definitionFit: Jim in Amis's novel is Lucky Jim, so the word describing him is lucky.

entries.clue: Editor is never, not ever, to change puzzle (9)

indicatorNotes.not ever: take the letters of ever out of never
indicatorNotes.to change: the letters are altered into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, taken as written
a deletion: NEVER with the letters EVER removed leaves N

annotation.surface: An editor insists the crossword must never ever be altered.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Editor' is not ED here: the whole word is fodder. 'Puzzle' is a verb, to confuse.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to leave someone confused about where they are is to puzzle them.
